extracted.intended_audience: municipal reformers, public-health officials, philanthropists, landlords and housing managers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical recommendations and evaluative standards for addressing the tenement‑house problem in New York: legal, managerial, design, sanitary, economic, and educational measures that make tenement improvement feasible and sustainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three effective methods for dealing with tenements
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three effective ways of dealing with the tenements in New York: I. By law. II. By remodelling and making the most out of the old houses. III. By building new, model tenements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private enterprise (conscience or business) must do the lion's share under the last two heads; law can rid worst plague-spots under strong public opinion but often moves slowly while the problem grows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal reform: make it unprofitable to own bad tenements
rubrics_metrics.description: To succeed, reform by law must aim at making it unprofitable to own a bad tenement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestions include arrest and summary punishment of persistent violators, licensing tenements to limit occupancy, or State regulation of rents. The law needs strong, steady public sentiment to back it; legislative remedies are apt to be slow and must be targeted to alter owners' incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remodel old houses with competent oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Remodelling and making the most out of old houses is an effective method when combined with competent onsite oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success requires thorough refitting (plumbing, light) and a competent janitor/housekeeper to enforce rules; examples include Miss Ellen Collins's Water Street houses where such measures produced order and acceptable financial returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build new model tenements with proper location and management
rubrics_metrics.description: Building new, model tenements is an effective remedy when properly located and intelligently managed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model tenements can be profitable if well managed; larger scale buildings, expert superintendence, and correct siting increase likelihood of success. Cited examples: Improved Dwellings Association, Tenement-house Building Company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair play between landlord and tenant; sustainable business model
rubrics_metrics.description: Housing the poor must be businesslike: 'fair play between tenant and landlord' with rents set 'as low as consistent with the idea of a business investment that must return a reasonable interest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charity, pastime, or fad will fail; schemes must exchange the tenant's money for what he can afford at reasonable price. Amateur philanthropy without business principles tends to fail and pauperize tenants.

rubrics_metrics.name: On‑site competent management (housekeeper/janitor/agent) is prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: A competent agent on the premises, a man (or housekeeper) of the best and highest stamp, who knows how to instruct and guide with a firm hand, is a prerequisite to the success of any reform tenement scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show dramatic improvement under strict, sympathetic housekeepers; absentee ownership without competent local management is a major obstacle. Competent caretakers enforce rules, prevent vandalism, and maintain improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical and sanitary standards: air, sunlight, plumbing, water
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical standards must be met: 'It is no longer lawful to construct barracks to cover the whole of a lot. Air and sunlight have a legal claim, and the day of rear tenements is past.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate dark unventilated bedrooms and open sewers; ensure sufficient water supply (especially in summer). Legal sanitary regulations have removed many worst features, but more work remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert management rather than amateur benevolence
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert management of model tenements succeeds where amateur management, with the best intentions, gives up the task as a flat failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional, experienced management is necessary to sustain improvements; insufficient supervision or premature withdrawal by owners can lead to relapse into worse conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and design matter: larger buildings and central yards
rubrics_metrics.description: The larger the scale upon which the model tenement is planned, the more certain the promise of success; small 25 × 100 lots make it 'impossible to secure the requirements of physical and moral health.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentration around central yards and larger blocks permit more air, sunlight, and reduced per-family supervision cost. Optimal designs avoid trying to cram many families into narrow limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate tenants and landlords; tenant conduct improves with opportunity and instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenants will respond to intelligent efforts when offered fair conditions and proper instruction; likewise, landlords need education to see that neglect kills tenants slowly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tenants provided with better accommodations and a competent caretaker adapted quickly and behaved better; public campaigns, missionary work, neighborhood guilds, and 'College Settlements' help create receptivity to improved conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cosmetic fixes; require substantive improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Cosmetic changes (a coat of paint and a tin cornice) do not remedy the underlying evils of crowding and filth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superficial improvements can mask persistent crowding and squalor; durable remedies require structural, sanitary, managerial, and economic changes rather than mere decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate economic viability with measured returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Model and reformed tenements can yield reasonable returns: examples report six to six and three-quarter percent, and on the whole about five and a half percent on invested capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial evidence (Miss Collins, Improved Dwellings Association) is used to counter the argument that decent housing for the poor cannot pay; emphasizing profit prospects helps attract private enterprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address absentee landlord problem by holding owners accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: Absentee landlords, managed by agents whose instructions are simply to collect rent or eject, are responsible for much trouble; remedy includes compelling owners to employ proper overseers or bringing them within jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Health Department's powers failed early where owners were remote; requiring a competent housekeeper or on‑site agent accountable to authorities would spare much suffering and enforcement trouble.
